name: Neck rings (Neck elongation)

card.summary: Stiff coils or rings worn around the neck, most famously by Kayan women, that make the neck look longer.
card.note: The effect is largely visual and comes from pressing the collarbone and ribs downward.

quick.overview:
Neck rings are rigid jewelry worn around the neck. In Kayan (Padaung) communities, girls begin wearing brass coils and add turns over the years, creating a very long-necked look that is a cultural mark of beauty and identity. Ndebele women in southern Africa wear rings called dzilla as a sign of marriage and status.

The lengthening is described as mostly illusory: the rings push the collarbone and upper ribs down, making the neck appear longer.
quick.how: Coils are wound on and added over years, starting in childhood. In looksmaxxing talk, neck elongation appears as an extreme example of how neck length changes proportions.
quick.risks: Reports note weight of coils up to about 5 kg, discomfort with rapid changes, and the practice's tourism pressures. The effects on the neck muscles and skeleton are examined in anthropological literature.

lead: Neck rings are stiff neck ornaments, as opposed to loose necklaces; the main forms are torcs and spiral coils.[1] European Iron Age men wore Celtic torcs as signs of wealth and status, an example being the Snettisham Torc from first-century BC England.[1]

The best-known case is the brass coils of Kayan (Padaung) women, which create a strikingly long neck. Girls may begin as young as two, though usually at five or six, with turns added up to around twenty and weights up to about 5 kg.[1] Marco Polo is said to have described the practice around 1300, and refugee practitioners in Thailand were open to tourists from 1984.[1]

According to Wikipedia the lengthening is mostly illusory: the coils push the collarbone and upper ribs down, though spaces between vertebrae may increase.[1] The South Ndebele wear copper or brass rings called dzilla; only married women wear them, traditionally given by husbands.[1]

chain: Coils press the collarbone and ribs downward
Elongated neck as a cultural beauty ideal
angle.text: Neck rings visually lengthen the neck by displacing the shoulder girdle downward. They are a cultural adornment and not a mainstream appearance method.

infobox: Kayan (Padaung), South Ndebele; torcs in Iron Age Europe

paras: Celtic torcs signaled wealth and status for men,[1] while Kayan women's coils are added turn by turn and Ndebele dzilla are stacked in multiples of three and also worn on arms and legs.[1]
The coils depress the clavicle and ribs, so the neck appears to stretch; vertebrae themselves do not lengthen.[1] An accelerated process around age twelve is described as painful.[1]
Tourism is often considered to encourage the practice in Myanmar.[1]
No studies found. A paleopathology paper on ethnology and skeletal deformations covers body-modification practices more broadly.[2]

timeline.event: Marco Polo is said to have described the practice to Western readers.[1]
Refugee practitioners in Thailand become accessible to tourists.[1]
